a: the land of Uz
p: Uz lay outside Israel, probably in Edom or north Arabia. The book's hero is not an Israelite.
b: The Bible links the name Uz with two families. Uz is a son of Aram in Genesis 10:23 and a nephew of Abraham in Genesis 22:21, which points north and east, toward Syria. But Uz is also a descendant of Seir the Horite in Edom (Genesis 36:28), and Lamentations 4:21 speaks of "daughter Edom, who lives in the land of Uz." Job's friend Eliphaz comes from Teman in Edom (2:11), and Jeremiah 25:20 lists "all the kings of the land of Uz" beside the Philistines and Edom. Most scholars therefore place Uz in Edom or the desert east of it. The Greek ending of Job (after 42:17) says Job lived "in the land of Ausitis, on the borders of Edom and Arabia." Either way the point is clear: Job is a man of the East, not of Israel.

a: his name was Job
p: Iyyov is a real ancient name. Its meaning is debated: 'Where is the Father?' or 'the hated one'.
b: The Hebrew Iyyov matches a West Semitic name found in texts of the second millennium BC: Ayyabum in documents from Mari and Alalakh, and Ayab, a ruler near Bashan in one of the Amarna letters (EA 256, about 1350 BC). Many scholars explain it as ayya-abu, "Where is the father?", a cry for a dead or absent father's help. Others hear the Hebrew oyev, "enemy": the one treated as hostile. The rabbis played on this when Job asks God, "Why do you treat me as your enemy?" (13:24, oyev), as if God had confused Iyyov and oyev (Bavli Bava Batra 16a). The name does not occur elsewhere in the Bible except in references to this Job (Ezekiel 14:14, 20; James 5:11).

a: wholehearted and upright
p: Tam means whole, complete, sound. It does not mean that Job never sinned.
b: The Hebrew tam describes something whole, with nothing missing. Used of people it means sincere and undivided, a person whose inside matches the outside: Jacob is called tam in Genesis 25:27, and Psalm 37:37 praises the tam. The KJV's "perfect" has led many readers to think the book claims Job was sinless. It does not; Job himself speaks of "the guilt of my young days" (13:26). The related noun tummah, "integrity" (2:3, 9; 27:5; 31:6), becomes one of the book's key words: the LORD praises it, Job's wife questions it, and Job refuses to let it go. Yashar, "upright," is literally "straight." The site renders tam of a person as "wholehearted" (content/terms.json); "blameless" is also fair.

a: He feared God and kept away from evil
p: Fearing God and turning from evil is the summary of wisdom in Proverbs and in Job 28:28.
b: The two phrases that close the verse are the core of Israel's wisdom teaching. "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge" opens Proverbs (Proverbs 1:7), and Proverbs 3:7 and 16:6 pair fearing the LORD with turning from evil. The poem on wisdom in Job ends with the same pair: "the fear of the Lord is wisdom, and to keep away from evil, that is understanding" (28:28). So the opening verse presents Job as the model of the wise man of Proverbs. The book then asks what happens when such a man loses everything: is his fear of God a bargain or a bond?

a: Seven sons and three daughters
p: Seven and three, seven thousand and three thousand, five hundred and five hundred: a perfect, rounded world.
b: Every number in 1:2–3 is a round number of fullness. Seven sons and three daughters make ten; seven thousand sheep and three thousand camels make ten thousand; five hundred pairs of oxen and five hundred donkeys make a thousand. Seven and ten are the Bible's numbers of completeness, and Ruth 4:15 and 1 Samuel 2:5 treat seven sons as the height of blessing. The storyteller paints an ideal life, and many scholars take the numbers as a sign of the tale's folk-story style. At the end, Job again has seven sons and three daughters, and twice the animals (42:12–13).

a: all the people of the East
p: The 'sons of the East' lived in the desert east of Israel and were famous for their wisdom.
b: Bene qedem, "the sons of the East," are the peoples of the Syrian and Arabian desert east of the Jordan: Jacob travels to their land (Genesis 29:1), and they raid Israel with Midian in Judges 6:3. They were known for wisdom: 1 Kings 4:30 says Solomon's wisdom was greater than "the wisdom of all the peoples of the east and all Egypt's wisdom" (1 Kings 4:30). To call Job the greatest of the people of the East is to make him the richest and most respected man in a region known for its sages.

a: on his day
p: 'His day' may be each son's birthday, or each son's turn in a week of feasts.
b: The Hebrew says only that each son held a feast "in his house, a man, his day." Some readers, ancient and modern, take "his day" as a birthday, since in 3:1 Job curses "his day," the day of his birth; several modern versions say "birthdays" outright. Others note that there are seven sons and suggest each took one day of the week, so that the feasting went round without end. That fits 1:5: "whenever the days of feasting had come full circle," and Job's offering may then have fallen on the eighth day. The Hebrew allows both readings, so the Plain English Translation keeps "his day."

a: make them holy
p: Job offers sacrifices himself, with no priest, temple or altar named, like Noah and Abraham.
b: Job "sanctifies" his children (qiddesh), probably by calling them to wash and prepare, as Israel did before Sinai (Exodus 19:10, 14), and then offers olot, "burnt offerings," one for each child; the Old Greek adds "and one calf for sin for their souls." In the law of Moses only priests offered on the altar; here the father of the family is priest, as in the stories of Noah (Genesis 8:20) and Abraham (Genesis 22:13). This is one reason many readers place Job in the age of the patriarchs. Job's priestly role returns at the end, when he offers for his friends and prays for them (42:8). The care he takes even for sins his children may have committed in secret shows how seriously he fears God.

a: cursed God in their hearts
p: The Hebrew says 'blessed God'. Scribes wrote 'bless' to avoid putting 'curse God' on the page.
b: Here and in 1:11, 2:5 and 2:9 the Hebrew verb is berakh, "bless," but the sense must be "curse": Job fears his children may have "blessed God in their hearts." This is a scribal euphemism, not a difference between manuscripts. Writers avoided setting the words "curse God" side by side, and wrote the opposite word instead, as in 1 Kings 21:10 and 13, where Naboth is accused of having "blessed God and the king." The Old Greek of 1:5 paraphrases ("they thought evil things against God"), but at 1:11 and 2:5 it keeps "bless." The euphemism sharpens the story: the real verb "bless" also appears (1:10, 21), and the question of the prologue is whether Job will bless God or "bless" him. When Job finally curses, he curses his own day (3:1), with a different verb.
orig: וּבֵרֲכוּ אֱלֹהִים (uverakhu Elohim), 'and they blessed God'

a: the sons of God
p: Heavenly beings who serve in God's court. The Greek calls them 'the angels of God'.
b: Bene ha'elohim, "the sons of God," are heavenly beings, members of God's court. They appear again in 2:1 and 38:7, where they shout for joy at creation, and similar phrases appear in Genesis 6:2, Psalm 29:1 and Psalm 89:6–7. "Son of" in Hebrew often means "member of a class": these are divine beings, not God's children in a family sense. The Old Greek translates "the angels of God" (see the variant), and that is how Jewish and Christian readers have mostly understood them. The scene is a council: the beings "take their stand" before the LORD like officials reporting to a king, as in 1 Kings 22:19–22 and Zechariah 6:5.

a: before the LORD
p: God's name YHWH appears in the prose story and the speeches from the storm, almost never in the debate.
b: "The LORD" in capitals stands for YHWH, the personal name of Israel's God, as in most English Bibles. In Job the name belongs to the narrator and to the scenes in heaven (1–2; 38:1; 40:1–6; 42:1–17), and Job uses it only in 1:21 and once in the poetry (12:9). The speakers in the debate, who are not Israelites, call God El, Eloah, Elohim and Shaddai, "the Almighty." The pattern tells the reader that the God whom these men of the East argue about is the LORD, Israel's God, even though they never name him so. When the LORD finally answers from the storm, the name returns (38:1).

a: The Accuser
p: In Job, ha-satan has the article: it is a title, 'the adversary', not yet a personal name.
b: Most English Bibles write "Satan" here, as if it were a name. The Hebrew is ha-satan, with the article: "the satan," "the adversary" or "the accuser." Hebrew does not put the article on personal names, so this is a role or office. The verb satan means to oppose or accuse (Psalm 109:4), and the noun is used of human opponents (1 Samuel 29:4; 1 Kings 11:14) and of the LORD's own angel blocking Balaam's road (Numbers 22:22, 32). In Zechariah 3:1–2 "the satan" stands at the right hand of the high priest to accuse him. Only in 1 Chronicles 21:1, without the article, does the word come close to a name. The Old Greek translated ho diabolos, "the slanderer," which gives English "devil." The site renders the title "the Accuser." See the views note at 1:7 and the book's opening pages.

a: From ranging across the earth
p: A loyal officer of God's court, the devil himself, or a figure in a story? Three main views.
b: A heavenly official. Many scholars and Jewish readers see the Accuser as one of God's servants, a prosecutor or inspector who roams the earth and reports to the king, much like the Persian king's "eyes and ears" (compare Zechariah 1:10–11). He tests on God's authority and cannot act without permission (1:12; 2:6). The Talmud says he "acted for the sake of heaven" (Bavli Bava Batra 16a), and also that "Satan, the evil inclination and the angel of death are one." The devil. Most Christian readers, from Gregory the Great to Calvin, identify him with Satan, God's enemy, "the accuser of our brothers" (Revelation 12:9–10), whose malice God bounds and turns to good. A story figure. Some read him as a literary device that voices the suspicion every reader feels: is goodness only self-interest? All agree that he disappears after chapter 2 and that the LORD never answers to him again.

a: my servant Job
p: The LORD gives Job the title of Moses and David. He uses it again four times at the end.
b: Avdi, "my servant," is a title of honor that the LORD gives to Abraham (Genesis 26:24), Moses (Numbers 12:7), David (2 Samuel 7:5) and the servant of Isaiah 40–55. Eved can mean a slave or a servant; in a king's mouth it means a trusted minister. The LORD calls Job "my servant" here, in 2:3, and four times in 42:7–8, so the title frames the whole book: whatever Job says in between, he is still the LORD's servant when the LORD speaks last.

a: Is it for no reason that Job fears God?
p: Chinnam, 'for nothing', is the key to the book: does anyone love God without being paid?
b: Chinnam means "for free, without cause, for nothing." The Accuser does not deny that Job is good; he denies that his goodness is free. Remove the reward, he says, and the piety will go. The LORD answers with the same word in 2:3: "you lured me against him, to swallow him up for no reason." Job will say God "piles up my wounds for no reason" (9:17). So the word runs both ways: Job's faith is tested to see if it is chinnam, and his suffering is chinnam too. The Mishnah asks the same question in its own way: it concludes from 13:15 and 27:5 that Job served God out of love, not only out of fear (Mishnah Sotah 5:5). It reads 13:15 with the Qere, "I will hope in him"; this site's Plain English Translation there follows the Ketiv (see the variant at 13:15). Many scholars think this question, more than "why do the righteous suffer?", is the book's starting point.

a: put a fence around him
p: The Accuser says God has put a fence around Job to protect him. Job will say God has fenced him in to trap him.
b: The verb sukh means to hedge or fence around. In the Accuser's mouth it is a fence of protection: nothing can touch Job, his household or his property. In 3:23 Job uses a close form of the same word, sakhakh, for a fence that traps him: he is a man "whom God has fenced in." The same fence that kept harm out now keeps Job in. The Plain English Translation uses "fence" in both verses so the echo can be heard. Compare 38:8, where God closed doors to hold back the sea.

a: touch everything he has
p: The verb 'touch' runs through the prologue and returns in Job's cry of 19:21.
b: The Hebrew naga', "touch, strike," ties the scenes together. The Accuser asks God to "touch" all Job has (1:11); the wind "touched" the house at its four corners (1:19); the Accuser asks God to "touch his bone and his flesh" (2:5). Eliphaz says that trouble has "touched" Job (4:5) and promises that harm will not touch him (5:19). Job, who never hears of the heavenly scene, sums it up in his own words: "God's hand has touched me" (19:21). The Plain English Translation keeps "touch" every time.

a: see if he does not curse you to your face
p: 'If he does not' is the start of a Hebrew oath: 'I swear he will curse you'.
b: The Hebrew reads "if not to your face he will curse you." This is the shape of a Hebrew oath, a self-curse with the penalty left unsaid: "(May such-and-such happen to me) if he does not curse you." It means "I swear he will curse you." The Plain English Translation keeps the "if" form as "see if he does not." The same oath form appears in 2:5 and is the frame of Job's great oath of innocence in chapter 31. On "curse," literally "bless," see the note at 1:5.
orig: אִם־לֹא עַל־פָּנֶיךָ יְבָרְכֶךָּ (im lo 'al paneikha yevarkhekka)

a: all he has is in your hand
p: The LORD allows the test but sets limits. Readers have long asked what that says about God.
b: The LORD neither strikes Job himself nor hands him over without limits: first all Job has, but not his body (1:12); then his body, but not his life (2:6). Traditional readers, Jewish and Christian, stress that God permits but does not do the evil, that he sets bounds, and that he trusts Job: the test proves to heaven and earth that faith can be free (Gregory, Aquinas, Calvin). Many modern readers find the wager troubling: ten children die to settle a question in heaven. Some answer that the prologue is a folk tale whose wager the poem later breaks open; others that the book itself feels the scandal, since the LORD admits he was "lured" against Job (2:3) and Job's protests are finally called right (42:7). The book never shows Job learning of the scene.

a: raiders from Sheba
p: Raiders from the south and from the east: the four disasters alternate between human enemies and fire and wind.
b: Sheva is Sheba, a people of Arabia, known as traders in Job 6:19 and Isaiah 60:6 and as raiders here. The Greek simply says "the captors." In 1:17 the attackers are Kasdim, Chaldeans, here not the later rulers of Babylon but the Chaldean tribes of south Mesopotamia whom Assyrian records call Kaldu from the 800s BC; the Greek has "the horsemen." The four blows alternate: raiders from the south, fire from the sky, raiders from the east, wind from the eastern desert. Human evil and natural disaster, from south, east and above: nothing is left.

a: Only I got away, just me, to tell you
p: Four messengers, each cut off by the next, each saying the same words: a storyteller's rhythm of catastrophe.
b: Each report ends with the same line, and each new messenger arrives while the last is "still talking" (1:16, 17, 18). The pattern makes the disasters fall faster than Job can take them in. The Hebrew stresses the survivor's loneliness: raq ani levaddi, "only I, by myself." Messengers who alone escape a disaster are a feature of ancient stories (compare the runner from the battle in 1 Samuel 4:12–17 and the survivor in Ezekiel 24:26). The young men killed in 1:15–17 are ne'arim, the same word used for Job's children in 1:19, "the young ones."

a: God's fire fell from the sky
p: Probably lightning. The messenger, without knowing it, blames God, just as the Accuser had asked God to strike.
b: "The fire of God" can be a way of saying a great fire, and here it is most likely lightning, as in the fire that fell on Elijah's altar (1 Kings 18:38) and on the soldiers of 2 Kings 1:10–12 (compare Numbers 11:1). The messenger names God as its source. The reader knows that the Accuser was given power over Job's property, yet the Accuser had asked God to "put out your hand" (1:11), and the LORD later says "you lured me against him" (2:3). The book does not let the reader settle who is the true author of the disasters; Job himself will say that the LORD took (1:21).

a: a great wind came from across the desert
p: Hot, violent winds from the eastern desert could flatten houses in the region.
b: The wind comes from "beyond the wilderness," the desert east of the settled land. The eastern desert wind, the sirocco or khamsin, can blow with great force (Jeremiah 4:11; 13:24; Hosea 13:15). This one "touched" the house at its four corners, a picture of a whirlwind striking from every side. A different word, se'arah, "windstorm," is used when the LORD answers Job (38:1). Readers have still connected the two storms: the God who speaks from the windstorm is the God of the wind that killed Job's children.

a: He ripped his cloak and shaved his head
p: Tearing clothes and shaving the head were standard signs of grief in the ancient Near East.
b: Tearing the outer robe (me'il, the garment of a man of rank, 1 Samuel 15:27) and shaving the head are mourning rites known across the region (Genesis 37:34; Isaiah 15:2; Jeremiah 41:5; Micah 1:16). The law of Moses forbids Israelites to shave their heads for the dead (Deuteronomy 14:1), but Job is not an Israelite and the story is set before or outside that law. Then he falls to the ground and "bows low," hishtachavah, the usual word for worship. His first response to disaster is grief and worship together.

a: naked I will return there
p: 'There' points to the womb of the earth: humans come from the ground and go back to it.
b: Job cannot return to his mother's womb, so "there" must mean the earth, pictured as the mother of all living (compare Psalm 139:15, "in the lowest parts of the earth," for the womb, and Genesis 3:19, "to dust you will go back"). Ecclesiastes 5:15 repeats the thought: "As he came out of his mother's womb, naked he will go back" (author's rendering), and Paul echoes it in 1 Timothy 6:7. The ancient Jewish writer Ben Sira speaks of the day people "are buried in the mother of all" (Sirach 40:1), the earth; there a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus and the Hebrew of manuscript B from the Cairo Genizah read "return", Job's verb. Job's saying is a proverb of human limits: nothing was his to begin with.

a: Let the LORD's name be blessed
p: Jewish law and Christian funerals both take up Job's words.
b: Job's words are the root of a Jewish practice. The Mishnah teaches that a person must bless God for the bad as for the good (Mishnah Berakhot 9:5), and on hearing of a death Jews say "Blessed is the true Judge." The prayer said at burial, the Tziduk ha-Din, "accepting the judgment," quotes 1:21. Christian burial services, including the Book of Common Prayer, read "The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away" at the graveside. The Old Greek adds a line before the blessing: "As it seemed good to the Lord, so it has happened." Note that Job says the LORD took, not the Sabeans or the Accuser: he holds God responsible, and blesses him anyway.

a: anything unfitting
p: Tiflah means something tasteless or improper. Job did not accuse God of acting unworthily.
b: Tiflah comes from a root meaning "tasteless, insipid" (the adjective tafel, "bland," is in 6:6). Applied to speech or conduct it means something unseemly or improper (Jeremiah 23:13; Job 24:12). The phrase "he did not give tiflah to God" means he did not charge God with acting in a way unworthy of God. The KJV's "nor charged God foolishly" catches the sense. By the end of the book Job will say far stronger things about God, which makes the LORD's final verdict that Job spoke rightly (42:7) all the more striking.

a: you lured me against him
p: God admits that the Accuser incited him. The rabbis said that if Scripture did not say it, no one could.
b: The verb hesit, "lure, incite, urge," is used of human persuasion (1 Samuel 26:19; Jeremiah 38:22). Here the LORD says it of himself, and the rabbis were startled: "Were it not written, it would be impossible to say it: like a man whom others incite, and he is incited" (Bavli Bava Batra 16a). The same verb appears when the LORD's anger "stirred David up" to take a census (2 Samuel 24:1), a deed that 1 Chronicles 21:1 credits to Satan. Some readers stress the LORD's honesty: he owns that Job suffers "for no reason" and takes responsibility. Others see God's freedom: he allows the test without being controlled. Others find here the book's first crack in any easy theology, a crack the poem will widen.

a: to swallow him up for no reason
p: Billa' is a strong word: to swallow, to devour, to ruin. And the LORD admits there was no cause.
b: Billa', "swallow," is used of the earth swallowing Korah (Numbers 16:30) and of enemies devouring Israel (Lamentations 2:2, 5). Here it describes what the Accuser has done to Job with God's permission. "For no reason" (chinnam) repeats the Accuser's word from 1:9: Job's piety has proved to be "for no reason," without reward, and so has his suffering, without fault. Job will use the same word in 9:17. See the note at 1:9.

a: Skin for skin!
p: A proverb whose exact sense is lost. The point is plain: a man will give anything to save himself.
b: No one is sure where the saying came from. Proposals include a barter phrase from the hide trade (one skin paid for another); a contrast between the outer skin and the inner skin, so that a man will give up his outer goods to keep his body; or "one skin for another": a man will let others' skins, even his children's, go to save his own. Rashi explains it as one part of the body given up for another, as a man throws up his arm to shield his head from a sword. Whatever its source, the second half explains it: "whatever a man owns, he will hand it over for his life." Job's loss of property and children proves nothing, says the Accuser; touch the man himself.

a: bad boils from the soles of his feet to his scalp
t: The boils of the covenant curse
p: Job's disease is described in the words of Deuteronomy 28:35, the curse on those who break the covenant.
b: Shechin ra', "bad boils," "from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head," is almost word for word the curse of Deuteronomy 28:35: "The LORD will strike you on the knees and legs with bad boils you cannot be healed of, from the soles of your feet to your scalp." The shechin was also the sixth plague of Egypt (Exodus 9:9–11) and Hezekiah's illness (2 Kings 20:7). A first reader would hear the echo: Job looks like a man under God's curse. That is exactly what his friends will conclude, and exactly what the reader knows is false. What disease is meant cannot be known; later symptoms (7:5; 19:20; 30:17, 30) have been read as elephantiasis, smallpox or a skin disease, and the Testament of Job adds worms.

a: right in the ashes
p: The Greek places Job on the dung heap outside the town, where the poor and outcast sat.
b: Sitting in ashes was a sign of mourning and humiliation (Jonah 3:6; Ezekiel 27:30; Esther 4:3). The Old Greek says Job "sat on the dung heap outside the city," the town's rubbish mound, and that is how Jewish and Christian tradition has pictured him. 1 Samuel 2:8 and Psalm 113:7 speak of God lifting the needy from the ash heap (ashpot), the place of the poorest. The man who once sat in the gate as a leader (29:7) now sits outside with the refuse. The clay shard was the nearest thing at hand to scrape the oozing sores.

a: Still holding on to your integrity?
p: She uses the very words the LORD used in heaven, but turns them into a question.
b: The LORD had said, "He still holds on to his integrity" (2:3). Job's wife, who cannot know that, says the same words: odkha machaziq betummatekha, "you are still holding on to your integrity?" What God praises she questions. Job will take the phrase up himself and make it his vow: "I will not set my integrity aside" (27:5) and "I have a grip on my righteousness" (27:6). The book thus sets three voices around one word: God's, his wife's and Job's.

a: Curse God, and die
p: Tempter, despairing mother, or the one who speaks the book's question? Readers have judged her very differently.
b: Tempter. Many Christian writers, from Augustine onward, made her the devil's helper: the Accuser took everything but left Job his wife, because she would serve his plan. Calvin calls her an instrument of Satan. Despairing. Others hear grief: she too has lost ten children, and she wants Job's agony to end, even at the cost of God's death sentence on a blasphemer. The Greek gives her a long lament that supports this reading (see the variant). Jewish tradition named her: the rabbinic Targum and the Talmud identify her as Dinah, Jacob's daughter (Bavli Bava Batra 15b), and the Testament of Job calls her Sitis. Modern readers often note that she first voices what Job will soon say himself. On "curse," literally "bless," see 1:5.

a: a godless woman
p: A naval is not a dim-witted person but someone who acts as if God did not matter.
b: Job compares his wife's words to those of "one of the nevalot." The naval in the Bible is not stupid but morally reckless: Nabal, who scorns David (1 Samuel 25:25); the one who says to himself, "There is no God" (Psalm 14:1); the disgraceful deeds called nevalah (Genesis 34:7; 2 Samuel 13:12). Job does not call his wife a fool; he says she is talking like the godless. He does not reject her, either: "Should we take the good from God," he says, and includes her.

a: Through all this Job did not sin with his lips.
p: Did Job sin in his heart? The rabbis debated the small change from 1:22.
b: In 1:22 the narrator says simply, "Job did not sin." Here he adds "with his lips." The Talmud records the view of Rava: "With his lips he did not sin, but in his heart he sinned" (Bavli Bava Batra 16a), and the rabbinic Targum reads the same way, "but in his heart he was already thinking words." Many other readers, Jewish and Christian, take "with his lips" as a full statement of innocence, since in Hebrew thought the lips express the heart (Psalm 39:1; Proverbs 10:19). Either way, the phrase prepares for chapter 3, where Job opens his lips.

a: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite
t: Three wise men of the East
p: Their names and towns point to Edom and Arabia, regions famous for wisdom.
b: Eliphaz is the name of Esau's firstborn, whose son was Teman (Genesis 36:4, 11). Teman, a town or region of Edom, was famous for its wise men (Jeremiah 49:7; Obadiah 8–9). Bildad the Shuhite may come from the family of Shuah, a son of Abraham and Keturah who was sent east (Genesis 25:2, 6). Zophar the Naamathite cannot be placed; Naamah in Judah (Joshua 15:41) is unlikely, and some suggest a place in north Arabia. The Old Greek makes them kings: Eliphaz "king of the Temanites," Bildad "tyrant of the Sauchaeans," Zophar "king of the Minaeans." They come as the wisest men of the East to sit with the greatest.

a: shake their heads with him
p: The verb nud is a gesture of sympathy: to rock or nod the head in grief with someone.
b: Nud means to sway or move to and fro, and as a gesture it shows sympathy with a mourner (Jeremiah 15:5; 16:5; Psalm 69:20; Isaiah 51:19). It is the right word for comforters: they come to share his grief bodily before they say anything. The same pair of verbs, "shake their heads with him and comfort him," returns in 42:11 for Job's brothers and sisters, who come only after the ordeal is over. Their first act is the one readers have praised most.

a: they tossed dust toward the sky, onto their heads
p: Throwing dust on the head was a sign of mourning. 'Toward the sky' recalls Moses and the boils of Egypt.
b: Putting dust or earth on the head was a common sign of grief and disaster (Joshua 7:6; 1 Samuel 4:12; 2 Samuel 1:2; Lamentations 2:10). Here the friends throw it "toward the sky," hashshamaymah, a detail some find odd. The only other place where someone throws something "toward the sky" with the same verb is Exodus 9:8–10, where Moses throws soot into the air and it becomes boils on Egypt. Some scholars suggest the friends' act is a rite meant to turn the evil away from themselves or to show they share Job's fate; most see simply a vivid picture of grief.

a: Seven days and seven nights
p: Seven days is the time of mourning. Jewish law learns here that comforters wait for the mourner to speak first.
b: Seven days was the time of mourning in Israel and among its neighbors (Genesis 50:10; 1 Samuel 31:13; Sirach 22:12), the origin of the Jewish week of mourning, shiva. The friends treat Job as a mourner, perhaps almost as one dead. The Talmud learns a rule from 2:13 and 3:1: "Comforters are not permitted to say anything until the mourner opens the conversation, as it says, 'After this Job opened his mouth,' and then 'Eliphaz the Temanite answered'" (Bavli Moed Katan 28b). Many readers count the friends' silence the wisest thing they do in the book.

a: cursed his day
p: Job curses, but not God. He curses his day, using qillel, the plain verb that the prologue avoided.
b: In the prologue the Accuser and Job's wife expected Job to "bless" (curse) God. Now Job does curse, and the narrator uses the plain verb qillel: but its object is "his day," the day of his birth (3:3), not God. The Accuser's prediction is both fulfilled and denied. Readers differ over whether chapter 3 is the beginning of Job's fall from the patience of 1–2 or an honest lament like those of the Psalms and Jeremiah that God never rebukes. Notice that Job never once in this speech names the LORD, and never speaks to God; he speaks about his day and about death.

a: Let it be lost, the day I was born
p: Jeremiah 20:14–18 also curses the day of birth. One poem probably knows the other.
b: Jeremiah's last lament says: "Cursed is the day I was born," and curses the man who brought his father the news, "A boy has been born to you, a son!" (Jeremiah 20:14–15, author's rendering). Job 3 shares the theme, the wish to have died in the womb, and the announcement of a male child. Most scholars think the Job poet knew Jeremiah and expanded his lament into a whole poem, which is one reason they date Job after Jeremiah; a few think the dependence runs the other way or that both draw on a common form. Job goes further than Jeremiah: he curses not only the day but the night of his conception, and he calls for the undoing of creation.

a: 'A male has been conceived.'
p: The night itself announces a boy. It is a poetic picture, not a reference to a person.
b: The Hebrew makes the night a speaker: the night "said, A gever has been conceived." A gever is a man, a strong male; the word is unusual for a baby and may be chosen on purpose, the man Job is now. The Old Greek, perhaps finding the speaking night odd, has "the night in which they said, Look, a male!" The night appears to know a secret that only God and the mother could know, which is why Job wants that night blotted out too (3:6–7).

a: That day: let there be darkness!
p: God said 'Let there be light' (Genesis 1:3). Job says 'Let there be darkness'.
b: The Hebrew yehi choshekh, "let there be darkness," turns God's first word at creation, yehi or, "Let there be light" (Genesis 1:3), on its head. Job goes on to wish that God "not ask after" the day, that light not shine on it, that darkness "reclaim" it, and that the night be shut out of the count of days and months (Genesis 1:14). Michael Fishbane argued that Job 3:3–13 takes up the creation days of Genesis 1 one by one to undo them, as Jeremiah 4:23–26 does: a spell against creation for one day. The divine speeches answer this chapter by taking Job back to the morning of creation (38:4–12).

a: God on high
p: Eloah, the singular of Elohim, is a poetic name for God found mostly in Job.
b: Eloah is the rare singular form of Elohim, "God." Of its roughly sixty uses in the Bible, more than forty are in Job, where the speakers use it alongside El and Shaddai. Elsewhere it is mostly poetic (Deuteronomy 32:15, 17; Psalm 18:31; Habakkuk 3:3, where Eloah comes "from Teman"). English has only one word, so the Plain English Translation renders Eloah, El and Elohim alike as "God"; the notes point out the name where it matters. Its use, like the names Uz and Teman, gives the dialogue an archaic, eastern color.

a: deep shadow
p: Tsalmavet was long read as 'shadow of death', as in Psalm 23:4. Many scholars now read 'deep darkness'.
b: The Masoretes pointed this word as tsalmavet, a compound of tsel, "shadow," and mavet, "death," and the Old Greek here and the KJV follow that: "the shadow of death." Many scholars think the word was originally tsalmut, "darkness," from a root known in Akkadian and Arabic, later reinterpreted as a compound. Others answer that the compound is old and that "death-shadow" fits Job's poetry, which pairs the word with death and Sheol (10:21–22; 38:17). Job uses it more than any other book (ten times). The Plain English Translation says "deep shadow," which keeps the darkness and leaves the hint of death to the note.

a: reclaim it
t: Darkness as the next of kin
p: Ga'al is the verb of the go'el, the family redeemer. Job asks darkness to claim the day as its own.
b: Ga'al usually means to buy back or reclaim something as next of kin, the work of the go'el (Leviticus 25:25; Ruth 4:4). Job pictures darkness as the day's rightful owner, taking back what was briefly lent to light. The Old Greek has "let darkness take it," and the KJV follows a second verb ga'al, "defile," with "stain it." The verb has a sad irony in this book: the same root gives the go'el whom Job will hope for in 19:25.

a: whatever blackens the day
p: A rare phrase, probably 'eclipses', the blackness that can fall on the day.
b: Kimrire yom is found only here. Many take it from kamar, "be black, be hot" (known in Syriac), so "blacknesses of the day": eclipses or sudden darkenings, which the ancient world feared as omens. Others take it from marar, "be bitter": "like the bitternesses of a day," that is, the worst things a day can bring (compare Amos 8:10). The Targum speaks of the bitterness of the day. The Plain English Translation's "whatever blackens the day" follows the first view.

a: Let it have no joy
p: The vowels say 'rejoice'. A small change gives 'be joined', which fits the line better.
b: The Masoretic vowels give yichad, from chadah, "rejoice": let the night have no joy among the days of the year. Many translators, including the KJV ("let it not be joined unto the days of the year"), read yechad, from yachad, "be united, be counted with," which matches the next line, "let it never come into the count of the months." The consonants allow both. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic vowels, which also fit 3:7, "let no glad shout come into it."

a: those who are ready to wake Leviathan
p: Job calls on the experts in curses, who can even rouse the chaos monster of the sea.
b: Leviathan (livyatan) is the coiling sea dragon of Canaanite myth, Litan in the Ugaritic texts, "the twisting serpent" defeated by Baal; the Bible uses him as a picture of chaos that God has mastered (Psalm 74:14; Isaiah 27:1; Job 41). Job imagines sorcerers who could put a curse on a day and even wake the monster that would swallow it, perhaps as an eclipse. The Old Greek has "the one who is about to subdue the great sea monster." Since Hermann Gunkel many scholars read yam, "Sea," for yom, "day": "those who curse the Sea," which pairs better with Leviathan. The Masoretic text has "day," and the Plain English Translation follows it. Job will meet Leviathan again, from God's side, in chapter 41.

a: the eyelids of dawn
p: The first light pictured as the dawn opening its eyes. The phrase returns for Leviathan's eyes in 41:18.
b: Afappe shachar, "the eyelids of dawn," pictures the first rays of morning as the opening eyes of the dawn, which some poets of Canaan treated as a god (Shachar, Isaiah 14:12). The only other use of the phrase is in 41:18, where Leviathan's eyes are "like the eyelids of dawn." Job wants the night of his conception never to see that dawn; the LORD will later describe the monster Job called up in 3:8 as having eyes that shine like it.

a: Why did knees meet me
p: A newborn was laid on the knees of the father or mother, a sign that the child was accepted.
b: A child born "on the knees" of a parent was acknowledged and received into the family (Genesis 30:3; 50:23; compare Isaiah 66:12). Whether the knees here are the father's, receiving the child as his own, or the mother's or the midwife's at birth, is debated. The second line moves to the mother's breasts. Job asks why anyone welcomed and fed him; if they had not, he would have died at once and found rest.

a: who raised up ruins for themselves
p: Kings 'build ruins': perhaps great tombs or pyramids, perhaps cities that are ruins now.
b: The line literally says the kings "built ruins (charavot) for themselves." It may mean that they rebuilt ruined places, a mark of royal glory (compare Isaiah 58:12; 61:4); that the great buildings they made are ruins now, an ironic comment on human greatness; or, as some propose, that charavot is a word for tombs or even Egypt's pyramids. The houses filled with silver in 3:15 may likewise be tombs stocked with treasure. In each reading the point is the same: in death the greatest lie as still as the stillborn.

a: There the wicked are done with turmoil
p: Job's picture of the world of the dead is peaceful: rest, equality and freedom.
b: In 3:13–19 Job imagines Sheol, the world of the dead, as a place of quiet: kings and stillborn babies lie together, prisoners no longer hear their driver, the slave is free. This is the opposite of the gloomy Sheol of 10:21–22 and of Isaiah 14:9–11, and Job's longing for it shows how bad life has become. It is not a doctrine of the afterlife but a cry: anything is better than this. Later in the book Job will wonder whether a man might live again (14:14) and hope to see God (19:25–27). Readers who find resurrection hope in Job read chapter 3 as the low point from which that hope rises.

a: they no longer hear the driver's shout
t: The voice of the slave driver
p: Nogesh is the word for the Egyptian slave drivers in Exodus.
b: The nogesh, "driver," is the taskmaster who forced Israel to make bricks in Egypt (Exodus 3:7; 5:6, 10–14). A reader who knew the Exodus would hear Job comparing life itself to slavery in Egypt. He uses the same picture of hard service in 7:1–2. Death, for Job, is the only exodus left.

a: Why does he give light to the sufferer
t: The one Job will not name
p: 'He' is God, but Job does not say so. 'Light' here means life.
b: The Hebrew says only "why does he give," or "why is light given." The giver must be God, and 3:23 names him (Eloah), but for most of the chapter Job avoids naming God and never addresses him. "Light" is a common Hebrew picture for life itself (33:30; Psalm 56:13): to "see the light" is to be born (3:16). Job's question is the question of every sufferer who wants to die: why keep someone alive whose life is only bitterness? The "bitter in soul" are people in deep grief (1 Samuel 1:10; 22:2).
orig: לָמָּה יִתֵּן לְעָמֵל אוֹר (lammah yitten le'amel or)

a: who would be glad to the point of shouting
p: The Hebrew 'to the point of joy' may hide the word for a grave mound.
b: The Hebrew reads hassemechim 'ele gil, literally "who rejoice to the point of joy (gil)." Many scholars revocalize gil as gal, "heap," here a burial mound or cairn: "who rejoice over the grave mound," which gives a neat parallel with "grave" in the second line (compare gal for a heap of stones over a body in Joshua 7:26). The Masoretic text, followed by the KJV and the Plain English Translation, simply piles up words for joy.

a: whom God has fenced in
t: The fence turned into a trap
p: Job uses the Accuser's word from 1:10, but the fence now traps him.
b: Job does not know what was said in heaven, yet his words answer it. The Accuser said God had "put a fence around" Job to protect him (1:10, sakhta); Job says God has "fenced him in" (vayyasekh) so that he cannot see his road. The protection that was supposed to make Job's faith easy has become, from where Job sits, a prison. Job uses the picture again in 19:8: "He has built a wall across my road; I can't get through." See the note at 1:10.

a: For I dreaded a dread, and it has reached me
t: Did Job's fear bring it on?
p: A popular idea says Job's fear caused his disasters. The verse says only that his worst fear came true.
b: Some popular teaching uses this verse to say that Job's fear opened the door to his troubles, so that fear is a kind of negative faith. The book does not say this: the prologue gives the cause, and the LORD twice says Job suffered "for no reason" (2:3). The verse may also be read in the present tense, "I fear a terror, and it comes on me": the dread of what might come next is part of Job's torment. Job's anxious care for his children (1:5) shows a man who knew how fragile his blessing was, not a man whose fear caused his loss. The Hebrew repeats the root: pachad pachadti, "I dreaded a dread."

a: Eliphaz the Temanite
p: Eliphaz begins gently and speaks from experience and revelation. His views deserve to be heard fairly.
b: Eliphaz is probably the oldest of the friends (compare 15:10), and he speaks first and longest. His first speech holds three main claims. One: the innocent do not perish; the wicked reap what they sow (4:7–11). Two: no human being is pure before God, as a voice told him in the night (4:12–21), so suffering is the lot of all. Three: Job should therefore seek God, accept his discipline, and expect restoration (5:8–27). Many readers find him the most courteous of the friends: he praises Job's past (4:3–4) and calls his piety his hope (4:6). Others hear condescension in his gentleness, and note that his words wound a man who has buried ten children. At the end the LORD says Eliphaz and his friends did not speak rightly of him (42:7), which the reader should keep in mind but not use to dismiss what is true in his words.

a: your wholehearted ways
p: Eliphaz uses the book's key word tom: Job's integrity should be his hope.
b: "Fear" here is yir'ah, short for the fear of God (compare 15:4), and "the wholeness of your ways" uses tom, the word for Job's integrity (1:1). Eliphaz is not accusing Job here; he reasons that if Job is the good man he seems, he has every reason to hope, because the upright are never wiped out (4:7). The trouble is the second half of that logic: if Job is not restored, he must not be upright. The friends begin with comfort and end with accusation (22:5) by following this same logic.

a: has an innocent man ever been lost?
p: Eliphaz states the teaching of reward and punishment. Parts of Scripture say the same; others question it.
b: Eliphaz's question assumes the answer "never." The same conviction appears in Psalm 37:25 (the righteous never forsaken), Proverbs 12:21 (no harm befalls the righteous) and the covenant blessings of Deuteronomy 28. Many readers note that Eliphaz states a real biblical truth as an absolute law, so that he can read a man's goodness from his fortunes. Ecclesiastes 7:15 denies it outright ("a righteous man perishes in his righteousness"), and Abel, the prophets and, for Christians, Jesus, are counterexamples. The book of Job as a whole sets this teaching beside the case it cannot explain.
r: Psalm 37:25; Proverbs 12:21; Deuteronomy 28:1–14; Ecclesiastes 7:15; Luke 13:1–5; John 9:2–3

a: whoever plows wickedness and plants misery gets a harvest of it
p: A farming proverb found across Scripture. Eliphaz implies it fits Job.
b: The picture of plowing and sowing evil and reaping the same is common wisdom: "Plant wrongdoing and you will harvest disaster" (Proverbs 22:8); "they sow the wind and reap the whirlwind" (Hosea 8:7; compare Hosea 10:13); and Paul's "whatever a person sows, that is what he will also reap" (Galatians 6:7). Eliphaz says "what I have seen": he appeals to experience. His words aven ("wickedness") and amal ("misery") are words Job used of his own life (3:10, 20); the hint is clear, though Eliphaz does not yet say it.

a: The roar of the lion, the snarl of the prowling lion
p: In two verses Eliphaz uses five different Hebrew words for lion. The fierce are broken.
b: The lines use aryeh (lion), shachal (a poetic word, perhaps a young or prowling lion), kefirim (young lions), layish (a mighty lion, 4:11) and lavi' (lioness). English cannot keep five words apart, so the Plain English Translation varies the descriptions. Lions stand for the violent wicked, who prey on others (Psalm 17:12; 58:6; Proverbs 28:15). Even they, Eliphaz says, are toothless and starving in the end. Some readers hear a veiled warning: Job's roaring (3:24, she'agah, the lion's word) will not save him.
orig: שַׁאֲגַת אַרְיֵה וְקוֹל שָׁחַל (sha'agat aryeh veqol shachal)

a: Now a message stole up to me
p: Eliphaz claims a private revelation, told in eerie detail. Is it true?
b: Eliphaz backs his teaching not only with experience but with an experience of the holy: a word that came by stealth, in a night vision, with dread, a breath on his face, hair standing on end, a shape he could not make out, and a hushed voice (4:12–16). It is one of the most vivid scenes of revelation in the Bible. Readers have judged it in different ways. Some take it as a true word from God, since its message, that no mortal is pure before God, appears in Scripture elsewhere (Psalm 143:2). Others note that the spirit is never identified and that its message contradicts God's own verdict on Job in 1:8, so it may be a deceiving spirit (compare 1 Kings 22:21–23) or a poetic parody of prophecy. Job later speaks of terrifying night visions sent by God (7:14), and Elihu describes God warning people in dreams (33:15–18).

a: at the hour deep sleep falls on mortals
p: Tardemah is the deep sleep God sent on Adam and on Abram before he spoke or acted.
b: Tardemah is not ordinary sleep but a deep, God-given sleep: on Adam when the woman was made (Genesis 2:21), and on Abram before the covenant between the pieces, with "a terror, a great darkness" (Genesis 15:12). Eliphaz's language places his vision among the great revelations of the past. The same Hebrew phrase returns word for word in Elihu's speech (33:15), which may be a deliberate echo.

a: A breath of wind slid past my face
p: Ruach can mean wind, breath or spirit. Eliphaz may feel a breeze, or see a ghost.
b: Ruach means wind, breath and spirit. Here it "passes" over Eliphaz's face and makes his hair bristle. Many translations write "a spirit," a ghostly being; others "a breath" or "a wind," the first sign of the presence before he sees the shape (4:16). The verb in 4:16 "it stood" has no clear subject, which adds to the eeriness. The Plain English Translation chooses "a breath of wind," the physical sensation, and leaves the reader with Eliphaz in the dark. Compare the "sound of a thin silence" before the voice that spoke to Elijah (1 Kings 19:12) and the "hush" of 4:16.

a: A hush, and a voice, I heard
p: The Hebrew 'silence and a voice' recalls the 'sound of a thin silence' that Elijah heard.
b: Demamah vaqol eshma' is literally "silence and a voice I heard," which can mean "there was a silence, then a voice" or "a hushed voice." The same word demamah is in 1 Kings 19:12, the qol demamah daqqah, "a sound of thin silence," in which the LORD came to Elijah. Eliphaz's vision borrows the hush of the true prophet's encounter. Whether his voice is equally true is the question the book raises.

a: 'Is any mortal in the right in God's sight?
p: The preposition min can mean 'more than' (KJV) or 'before, in the eyes of' (most modern versions).
b: The Hebrew haenosh me'eloah yitsdaq uses min, which can mean "from," "more than" or "in comparison with." The KJV reads "Shall mortal man be more just than God?", which no one would claim and which seems too obvious to need a revelation. Most modern translators read "before God" or "in God's sight": can any human be right with God? That is the question Job himself asks in 9:2, and the friends repeat in 15:14 and 25:4. "Be in the right" (tsadaq) has a legal flavor: to win one's case, to be declared innocent. It is also unclear where the spirit's words end: after 4:17, or after 4:21, as the Plain English Translation takes it.

a: even in his messengers he finds error
p: If God finds fault even in his angels, what hope for humans? The word for 'error' occurs only here.
b: God's "servants" and "messengers" (mal'akhim, "angels") are the heavenly beings of 1:6. The word for what God charges them with, toholah, is found nowhere else; it is usually explained as "error" or "folly," perhaps related to holelot, "madness" (Ecclesiastes 1:17). Eliphaz is not saying the angels have rebelled, but that even they fall short beside God, so humans, made of clay, fall shorter still. Eliphaz repeats the argument in 15:15. Later Jewish and Christian readers linked such verses with the fall of rebel angels (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6).

a: those who live in houses of clay
p: The body is a clay house founded on dust, as fragile as a moth.
b: Humans live in "houses of clay" because God formed them from the ground (Genesis 2:7); Job says God shaped him "like clay" (10:9; compare 33:6). Their foundation is "in the dust," and they are crushed "before a moth," a hard phrase that may mean "as easily as a moth," "sooner than a moth," or "before the moth" (as a moth eats away a garment, 13:28). Paul uses the same picture for the body as a tent and clay jar (2 Corinthians 4:7; 5:1).

a: When the rope of their tent is pulled up
p: Yeter may be a tent cord pulled up, a picture of death, or 'what is left over', as the KJV read it.
b: Yitram may come from yeter, "cord, bowstring" (Judges 16:7; Psalm 11:2), giving the image of a tent that collapses when its rope is pulled up, a common ancient picture of death (Isaiah 38:12; 2 Corinthians 5:1). The KJV took yeter in its other sense, "excess, excellence": "Doth not their excellency which is in them go away?" The tent picture fits the "houses of clay" of 4:19 and is followed by most modern translators. "With no wisdom" means they die without ever grasping why.

a: Which of the holy ones will you look to?
p: The 'holy ones' are heavenly beings. Eliphaz says none of them will take Job's side.
b: Qedoshim, "holy ones," are members of God's heavenly court (Psalm 89:5, 7; Deuteronomy 33:2–3; Zechariah 14:5; Daniel 4:17). Eliphaz challenges Job: call out, if you like, but no heavenly being will answer, since even they are found wanting (4:18). His words anticipate a hope Job will reach for again and again: an umpire between him and God (9:33), a witness in heaven (16:19), a redeemer (19:25). Eliphaz rules it out; Job will not give it up. Elihu later speaks of an angel who might plead for a person (33:23).

a: For bitterness slays the fool
p: Ka'as is grief that turns into anger. Job picks up the word in 6:2.
b: Ka'as is vexation, a smoldering mix of grief and resentment (1 Samuel 1:6–7 uses it of Hannah's torment). Qin'ah is passion: jealousy, zeal, envy. The "fool" (evil) and the "naive" (poteh) are the stock bad examples of Proverbs. Eliphaz's proverb is a warning: Job's outburst in chapter 3 is the kind of thing that destroys a person. Job answers by asking that his ka'as be weighed (6:2): it is not folly but the true weight of his suffering.

a: I cursed his homestead
p: Why would Eliphaz curse a man's home? The Greek and some scholars read 'it rotted' or 'was cursed'.
b: The Hebrew va'eqqov naveihu says "I cursed his pasture (or homestead)." Many find it odd that Eliphaz would curse the fool, and the Old Greek has instead "but at once their way of life was eaten up." Some scholars change one letter to read "it was cursed" or take the verb from a different root meaning "rot." Others keep the Hebrew and explain it as declaring cursed: when Eliphaz saw the fool's sudden ruin, he recognized it as God's curse. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew. Either way the point is that the prosperity of the wicked is short. Job will flatly deny this in 21:7–18.

a: His sons are a long way from rescue
p: Eliphaz speaks of the fool's children crushed and his harvest taken. Job's own children were just killed.
b: Eliphaz describes the fate of the fool in general terms: his sons crushed with no one to save them (5:4), his harvest eaten by others (5:5). He may mean nothing personal. But to a man whose ten children were just crushed by a falling house and whose herds were taken by raiders, the words cut close. Some commentators think Eliphaz is tactless but sincere; others that the poet lets the reader hear an accusation the friends are not yet ready to say aloud. Bildad will say it outright: "If your children sinned against him..." (8:4).

a: They are trampled in the town gate
p: The gate of an ancient town was its law court. To be crushed in the gate is to lose one's case.
b: In Israel and its neighbors the elders sat in the town gate to judge cases (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1–2; Amos 5:10–15). To be "crushed in the gate" is to be ruined in court, with "no one to rescue," that is, no one to plead one's cause. Job remembers his own days as a judge in the gate, when he rescued the poor (29:7, 12–17). His fear of being condemned without a defender echoes through the book (9:33; 31:21).

a: the sons of flame fly up high
p: The 'sons of Resheph' may be sparks, birds or plague demons. Resheph was a god of fire and plague.
b: The Hebrew says bene reshef, "the sons of Resheph." Resheph was a Canaanite god of plague and fire, known from Ugarit and Phoenicia; in the Bible the word means flame or pestilence (Deuteronomy 32:24; Psalm 78:48; Habakkuk 3:5). Most readers take "the sons of flame" as sparks, which rise by nature, so trouble is as natural to humans as sparks to fire (KJV). The Old Greek has "the young of the vulture fly to the heights," and some moderns read birds or demons. Some scholars also read yolid, "man begets trouble," for yulad, "is born for trouble," which fits 5:6: trouble does not grow from the soil; humans produce it. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic vowels.

a: If it were me, I would turn to God
p: Seek God and leave your case with him: good advice in itself, which Job takes in a way Eliphaz never meant.
b: Darash el, "seek, turn to," is the language of prayer and repentance (Psalm 34:4; Isaiah 55:6). Eliphaz's advice is pious and, in its place, sound: bring your case to God, who does wonders, lifts the lowly and frustrates the crafty (5:9–16). Christian and Jewish readers have often quoted it for comfort. The irony is that Job does exactly this: he lays his case (mishpat, 13:18) before God, demands an answer and gets one (38:1). But Eliphaz means "submit and repent," while Job means "argue my innocence." The LORD's final verdict favors Job's way (42:7).

a: He does great things, beyond searching out
p: Job quotes Eliphaz's line almost word for word in 9:10, but gives it a darker meaning.
b: In 9:10 Job says, almost word for word, that God "does great things beyond searching out, marvels without number." For Eliphaz this is comfort: God's power is used to lift the lowly (5:11). For Job it is terror: God's power is so great that no one can hold him to account (9:11–12). Psalm 145:3 uses a similar phrase in praise. The same truth, God's unsearchable greatness, is heard differently by the comfortable and the crushed; the LORD's speeches in 38–41 will show it in a third light.

a: He snares the wise in their own cunning
p: Paul quotes this line in 1 Corinthians 3:19, the only direct quotation of Job in the New Testament.
b: Paul writes: "For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. It is written: 'He catches the wise in their cunning'" (1 Corinthians 3:19). His Greek is not the Septuagint's ("he who takes the wise in their understanding") but is closer to the Hebrew, which suggests he knew another Greek form or translated it himself. The quotation raises an old question: Paul cites as Scripture a line from Eliphaz, whose speeches the LORD says were not right (42:7). Most interpreters answer that the friends say many true things and misapply them; the verse is true, but not of Job.

a: from the sword, from their mouths
p: The Hebrew is abrupt: 'from the sword, from their mouth'. It may mean the sword that is their mouth.
b: The Masoretic text reads mecherev mippihem, "from the sword, from their mouth," with no link between the two. Many take it as "from the sword of their mouth," that is, slander and false accusation, a common picture (Psalm 57:4; 64:3), which fits the "lash of the tongue" in 5:21. Others emend the text to give a noun parallel to "the needy," such as "the orphan" or "the desolate." The KJV kept the Hebrew as it stands, as the Plain English Translation does.

a: Think how fortunate a man is when God corrects him!
p: Suffering as a father's discipline: a theme of Proverbs and Hebrews, and of Elihu in Job 33–36.
b: Ashre, "how fortunate, happy," begins many sayings in the Psalms (Psalm 1:1; 94:12, "Happy is the man whom you discipline, LORD"). Eliphaz's saying is very close to Proverbs 3:11–12, which Hebrews 12:5–11 quotes: the LORD disciplines those he loves, as a father his son. This is the friends' kindest explanation of suffering: not punishment but correction, meant to heal (5:18). Elihu develops it at length (33:14–30; 36:8–15). It is a real biblical truth; the book's question is whether it explains Job, whom God called wholehearted before the trouble began.

a: the Almighty's
p: Shaddai, an old name of God from the patriarchs' time, appears 31 times in Job.
b: Shaddai is the name by which God appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Genesis 17:1; Exodus 6:3), and Job uses it more than any other book, 31 of about 48 times. Its meaning is uncertain: "the one of the mountain" (from Akkadian shadu, mountain), "the one of the breasts" (from shad, breast, a God of fertility, compare Genesis 49:25), or, as the rabbis explained it, "the one who is sufficient" (she-dai). The Greek often has pantokrator, "ruler of all," from which comes the traditional English "the Almighty," the rendering this site uses. Its frequency in Job is part of the book's ancient, patriarchal color.

a: He is the one who causes pain, and he bandages
t: The God who wounds and heals
p: Eliphaz echoes the Song of Moses and Hosea: the same God strikes and heals.
b: Deuteronomy 32:39 has God say, "I strike down, and I make well" (Deuteronomy 32:39), and Hosea 6:1: "it was he who tore us apart, and he will heal us. He struck us, and he will bandage us." Compare 1 Samuel 2:6–7. Eliphaz uses this confession to give Job hope: the God who struck him will mend him. The Hebrew writes "his hand" in the consonants and "his hands" in the margin (the Qere); the Plain English Translation follows the Qere.

a: Through six troubles he will save you,
p: A numerical saying: 'six, even seven' means 'every trouble, however many'.
b: The pattern "x, and then x+1" is a favorite device of Hebrew and Ugaritic poetry (Proverbs 6:16; 30:15, 18, 21, 29; Amos 1:3–2:6). It means "many, indeed all." Eliphaz then lists seven troubles: famine, war, the lash of the tongue, havoc, hunger again, wild animals and, implied, loss in the field and flock (5:20–24). To a man who lost everything in one day, the promise that no trouble will "touch" him (see 1:11) sounds hollow, but Eliphaz means it as encouragement.

a: The stones in the field will be bound to you by covenant
p: Peace with the stones means fields free of rocks. The rabbis read 'stones' as a strange wild creature.
b: The idea is that nature will be at peace with the righteous: the stones will not spoil his fields and the wild animals will not attack him, like the covenant with the creatures promised in Hosea 2:18 and Ezekiel 34:25 (compare Isaiah 11:6–9). Rashi connects avne hassadeh with the adne hassadeh, "lords of the field," a mysterious man-like wild creature mentioned in the Mishnah (Kilayim 8:5); some moderns likewise suggest "field spirits." Most translators keep "stones."
orig: עִם־אַבְנֵי הַשָּׂדֶה בְרִיתֶךָ ('im avne hassadeh veritekha)

a: miss nothing
p: The verb is chata', which usually means 'sin'. Its root meaning is 'miss the mark'.
b: Velo techeta means "and you will not miss" (find nothing missing), using chata', the ordinary Hebrew word for "sin," in its basic sense of missing a target (Judges 20:16). A Hebrew ear might hear a second meaning: "and you will not sin." Eliphaz promises the man who returns to God a safe tent, a full flock and, perhaps, a life without fault.

a: Still strong, you will go down to your tomb
p: Kelach is a rare word, perhaps 'full vigor' or 'ripe old age'. Job will have both (42:16–17).
b: Kelach occurs only here and in 30:2. It is usually explained as vigor or ripeness, so "in full strength" or "in ripe old age." Eliphaz pictures a good death: the righteous are gathered in like grain at harvest. The sheaves "go up" to the threshing floor, perhaps with a hint of the funeral procession. Eliphaz's promise comes true in its own way: Job dies "old and satisfied with days" (42:17), though not by the route Eliphaz imagined.

a: we have studied it, and that is how it is
p: Eliphaz speaks for the friends and for generations of wise men. Tradition versus experience.
b: "We" shows that Eliphaz speaks for the friends and for the accumulated wisdom of the sages (compare 8:8–10; 15:9–10, 18). It is the voice of tradition tested over time, and it deserves respect: much of it is in Proverbs. Job's reply in chapters 6–7 sets his own experience against it. Many readers see in this exchange the book's central tension: received wisdom, true in general, against one man's case that it does not fit. Carol Newsom calls the book a "contest of moral imaginations" between such voices.

a: The Almighty's arrows are stuck in me
p: Job pictures God as an archer whose poisoned arrows have struck him.
b: God as a warrior with arrows is an old biblical picture (Deuteronomy 32:23, 42; Psalm 7:12–13; Psalm 38:2; Lamentations 3:12–13). Job uses it of himself: the arrows are poisoned, and his spirit drinks the venom. He will repeat the image in 16:13: "His bowmen ring me in." In Canaanite religion Resheph, whose "sons" Eliphaz mentioned in 5:7, was an archer god of plague, and some readers hear a link: Job's sickness is not natural trouble but the arrows of Shaddai himself. Job is the first speaker in the book to say plainly that God is attacking him.

a: Will a wild donkey bray if it is standing in grass?
p: Animals only bellow when something is wrong. Job's cries have a cause.
b: Job answers Eliphaz's warning about the fool's bitterness (5:2) with a farmyard proverb: a donkey does not bray, nor an ox bellow, when it has food. If Job cries out, it is because he is starving, not because he is a fool. The wild donkey reappears in 39:5–8, where the LORD describes it roaming free and scorning the city's noise.

a: the slime of purslane
p: No one knows the exact food. Proposals: the sap of a plant, or the white of an egg.
b: Rir challamut is found only here. Rir is slime or saliva (1 Samuel 21:13); challamut has been explained as a plant, purslane or mallow, whose sap is slimy and tasteless (from Syriac and later Jewish usage), or as the yolk or white of an egg, as the Targum and Rashi take it, from which comes the KJV's "the white of an egg." The Old Greek reads it as "empty words." The general sense is clear: tasteless, sickening food. "Bland" (tafel) is the word behind "unfitting" in 1:22. Readers differ over what the food stands for: Job's suffering, which he cannot stomach, or his friends' counsel, which has no salt.

a: they are like disease in my bread
p: The phrase kidvei lachmi, 'like the sickness of my bread', is very hard to explain.
b: The second line reads hemmah kidvei lachmi, "they are like the sicknesses of my bread." Devai, "sickness, loathsomeness," is rare (Psalm 41:3), and the whole line has been read many ways: "they are like loathsome food to me," "they are the sickness of my food," or, with small changes, "my inward parts loathe them." The KJV's "as my sorrowful meat" is another guess. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew images. Whether "they" are Job's sufferings or the friends' bland words (6:6) is also unclear.

a: that he would free his hand and cut me off
t: A prayer for death, not a plan for suicide
p: Job asks God to end his life. He never speaks of taking it himself.
b: Betsa' is the weaver's word for cutting the finished cloth from the loom; Hezekiah uses it of death in Isaiah 38:12: "he snips me off the loom." Job asks God to "free his hand," to stop holding back, and finish him. Readers have often noted that Job, for all his longing for death (3:21; 7:15), never considers suicide; he leaves life and death in God's hands, as do Moses (Numbers 11:15), Elijah (1 Kings 19:4) and Jonah (Jonah 4:3, 8). Jewish and Christian teachers have used Job to show that a cry for death is not a sin, while taking one's own life is a different matter.

a: I would spring up in pain that does not spare
p: Two rare words make this line uncertain: 'leap for joy' or 'recoil', and 'that does not spare' or 'let him not spare'.
b: Va'asalledah occurs only here. It is usually taken as "I would leap" (for joy, from later Hebrew and Arabic), but the Old Greek has "I leaped," the rabbis and the KJV "I would harden myself," and some moderns "I would recoil." Lo yachmol can describe the pain ("pain that does not spare") or God ("let him not spare," KJV). The comfort Job wants is to die before he gives up: "I have not hidden the sayings of the Holy One," that is, he has not denied or concealed God's words (kiched, "hide, deny"). The Holy One (qadosh) is a title of God common in Isaiah.
orig: וַאֲסַלְּדָה בְחִילָה לֹא יַחְמוֹל (va'asalledah vechilah lo yachmol)

a: A man who is melting away should have loyal love from his friend
p: One of the hardest lines in Job. Most read: a friend owes loyalty even to one who loses his faith.
b: The Hebrew reads lammas mere'ehu chesed / veyir'at Shaddai ya'azov, literally "to the one melting, from his friend, loyal love; and the fear of Shaddai he forsakes." Lammas is uncertain ("the one melting," despairing). The Plain English Translation follows the most common reading: a friend owes hesed, loyal love, even to someone so crushed that he lets go of the fear of God. A second reading, supported by the Targum and Vulgate, changes lammas to "one who withholds": "whoever withholds loyal love from a friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty." A third takes the second line as the result: without a friend's loyalty, the despairing man will give up God. The Old Greek reads quite differently. Hesed is the covenant word for faithful love (content/terms.json).

a: My brothers have betrayed me like a wadi
p: A wadi runs with snowmelt in winter and is dry when travelers need it most in summer.
b: A nachal, wadi, is a desert streambed. In the rainy season it roars with water, dark with melting ice and snow from the hills (6:16); in summer it vanishes, sinking into the sand or winding off into the waste (6:17–18). Caravans from Tema and Sheba, crossing the Arabian desert, count on finding water there and find nothing (6:19–20). Job's friends are like that: full of words, dry when he needs them. Jeremiah uses the same picture of God in his bitterness: "You have become for me like something that deceives, like waters that cannot be trusted?" (Jeremiah 15:18, author's rendering).

a: Their courses twist and turn
p: The same Hebrew letters mean 'paths' or 'caravans'. Many read: caravans turn off their road and die.
b: The word orchot can be read as "paths" (the Masoretic vowels) or as orchot with another sense, "caravans," as in 6:19. On the first reading, the streams themselves wind away and vanish into the wasteland, as the Plain English Translation and the KJV have it. On the second, which many modern versions prefer, caravans turn aside from their route to look for water, wander into the desert and perish. Both pictures fit the passage.

a: The caravans from Tema
p: Tema was a great oasis of north Arabia; Sheba, a trading people of the south.
b: Tema (modern Tayma in northwest Saudi Arabia) was an oasis town on the incense road (Isaiah 21:14; Jeremiah 25:23). The Babylonian king Nabonidus lived there for about ten years (about 552–543 BC), and inscriptions of his time have been found at the site. Sheba was the trading kingdom of south Arabia, famous for its caravans of incense and gold (1 Kings 10:1–2; Isaiah 60:6; Ezekiel 27:22). Job's world is the world of the Arabian trade routes.

a: Have I ever told you, 'Give me a present'?
t: What Job asked of his friends
p: Job did not ask for money, ransom or rescue. He asked only for loyalty.
b: Job lists what friends might be asked for in a crisis: a gift, a bribe paid on his behalf, rescue from an enemy, a ransom from tyrants (6:22–23). He has asked none of these. He wanted only hesed (6:14): that they stay with him and hear him. The words "rescue" and "buy back" (padah) are the language of the redeemer; later Job, having found no help on earth, will look for a redeemer in heaven (19:25).

a: How sharp the words of honesty are!
p: Nimrats can mean painful, forceful or sickening. Some read 'how sweet', with one letter changed.
b: Nimretsu comes from a root used of a "grievous" curse (1 Kings 2:8) and "sickness" (Micah 2:10). Job may mean "how painful are honest words", ironically: you call your words honest, but they only hurt; or "how forceful are honest words, but what does your scolding prove?" Some scholars read nimletsu, "how sweet" (as in Psalm 119:103): honest words would be welcome, but yours are not honest. The second line plays on hokhach, "correct, argue": "what does your correcting correct?" Job wants real arguments, not reproof.

a: You would cast lots over a fatherless child
p: Orphans could be seized for debt. Job says his friends treat him as heartlessly.
b: Casting lots over people was what conquerors did with captives (Joel 3:3; Obadiah 11; Nahum 3:10). A widow's children could be taken as slaves for a debt (2 Kings 4:1), and the law and the prophets repeatedly defend the fatherless (Exodus 22:22; Isaiah 1:17). Job accuses his friends of treating him the way the worst creditors treat orphans: as property to bargain over. Later Eliphaz will accuse Job of exactly this sin (22:9), and Job will swear he never did it (31:17, 21).

a: Think again, please, and do no injustice
p: Shuvu means 'turn' or 'repent'. Job turns the call to repent back on his friends.
b: Shuvu is the verb of repentance, "turn back" (Isaiah 55:7; Jeremiah 3:12). Eliphaz implied that Job must turn to God; Job tells the friends to turn instead, to reconsider before they wrong him. At the second "think again" the consonants have shuvi, a singular form, and the margin (Qere) shuvu, plural; the Plain English Translation follows the Qere, though the sense is the same. "My being in the right" (tsidqi) is a legal phrase: Job's case still stands.

a: a term of hard duty
p: Tsava means army service or forced labor. The same word describes Jerusalem's suffering in Isaiah 40:2.
b: Tsava is military service, a fixed term of hard duty under orders, or forced labor. Job pictures human life on earth as conscription: no rest, no choice, only the wait for discharge. He uses the word again in 14:14, where the Plain English Translation also has "hard duty." Isaiah 40:2 uses the same word for Jerusalem's exile: "her term of service (tsava'ah) is over," and announces she has received "double" for all her sins. Readers who place Job after the exile hear the two passages together.

a: like a worker hoping for his wages
p: A hired worker longed for the evening shade, when the work ended and the day's pay came.
b: The law required that a hired worker be paid at the end of each day, before sunset (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15; compare Matthew 20:8). The slave longs for the shade of evening, the end of labor; the hired man for his pay. Job has neither: he works through months of nothing and receives only nights of trouble (7:3). His picture of himself as a hired hand cheated of wages is a cry against God's justice.

a: So I have inherited months of nothing
p: Nachal means to receive as an inheritance. Job's inheritance is 'months of nothing'.
b: Honchalti is "I have been made to inherit." An inheritance (nachalah) is a gift that stays in the family, the land or the blessing. Job's share is shav', emptiness or worthlessness (the word of the commandment against taking God's name "in vain," Exodus 20:7). It is "months": Job's suffering has lasted far longer than the week of 2:13. At the end of the book Job gives his daughters an inheritance with their brothers (42:15).
orig: הָנְחַלְתִּי לִי יַרְחֵי־שָׁוְא (honchalti li yarche shav')

a: The evening stretches on
p: Middad 'erev is uncertain: 'the evening drags on' or 'when will evening be measured out?'
b: The Hebrew umiddad 'arev is unusual. Most take middad from madad, "measure, stretch": "the evening is long," the night drags on. Others read it as a question parallel to the first line, "when will the evening be over?", or emend to middey 'erev, "as often as evening comes." The general picture is clear: the sick man's night will not end.

a: they run out, with no hope left
p: Tiqvah means both 'hope' and 'thread'. Job's days run out like thread on a weaver's shuttle.
b: The weaver's shuttle (ereg) flies back and forth across the loom. Job's days fly faster, and they come to an end be'efes tiqvah, "without hope." But tiqvah also means "cord, thread" (Joshua 2:18, 21, Rahab's scarlet cord). So the line carries a double picture: the shuttle stops when the thread is used up, and Job's life ends when hope runs out. The Plain English Translation's "run out" lets English feel both. Compare Hezekiah's weaving picture of death in Isaiah 38:12.

a: Keep in mind that my life is wind
p: For the first time Job addresses God directly. From here on he speaks to God as much as about him.
b: "Remember" is a command in the second person masculine singular. Job is not speaking to the friends now but to God, for the first time in the book. He reminds God of how fleeting human life is, "wind" (ruach), as the psalms do (Psalm 78:39; 89:47; 103:14–16). The move from talking about God to talking to God is one of the great turns in the book: the friends never pray, but Job does, even when his prayer is a complaint. At the end the LORD says Job spoke rightly "to me" or "of me" (42:7, the Hebrew allows both).
orig: זְכֹר כִּי־רוּחַ חַיָּי (zekhor ki ruach chayyai)

a: the one who goes down to Sheol never climbs back up
p: Sheol is the world of the dead under the earth. Job says no one returns from it.
b: She'ol is the Hebrew name for the place of all the dead, good and bad, pictured as deep under the earth, dark and silent (10:21–22; 17:13–16). The site leaves it as "Sheol." In 7:9–10 Job states the common belief of his world that no one comes back: like a cloud that thins away, the dead do not return to their homes (compare 2 Samuel 12:23; Psalm 103:16). Later he will wonder aloud, "When a man dies, can he come back to life?" (14:14). The Old Testament's fuller hope of resurrection comes most clearly in Daniel 12:2.

a: Am I the Sea, or am I the Dragon
p: Job asks if God takes him for the chaos monster that the gods of the myths had to guard.
b: Yam, "Sea," and tannin, "Dragon," are the forces of chaos in Canaanite myth. In the Ugaritic Baal stories Baal defeats Yam, the Sea, and the goddess Anat boasts of muzzling Tunnan, the dragon. In the Babylonian creation epic Enuma Elish, Marduk splits the sea goddess Tiamat and posts guards so that her waters cannot escape. The Bible uses the same pictures for the LORD's power over the sea (Psalm 74:13; Isaiah 51:9; Job 26:12; 38:8–11). Job asks bitterly whether God thinks him so dangerous that he must be watched night and day. The LORD's speeches answer by showing how he does guard the sea (38:8–11) and how he plays with Leviathan (41).

a: then you break me down with dreams
p: Eliphaz received a holy vision by night. Job's nights bring only terrifying dreams.
b: Eliphaz told of a night vision that gave him wisdom (4:12–16). Job says God sends him night visions too, but they only terrify him. The word "visions" (chezyonot) is the same as Eliphaz's (4:13). Some readers think Job is mocking Eliphaz's revelation; others that he is simply describing the nightmares of a sick man, which he, like everyone in his world, takes as coming from God. Either way, Job's bed, which should comfort him (7:13), has become a place of terror.

a: and would pick death over my bones
p: The Hebrew says death rather than 'my bones'. Many emend to 'my pains'.
b: The Masoretic text has mavet me'atsmotai, "death rather than my bones": death is better than this wasted body, a skeleton of a life (compare 19:20). Many scholars change one letter to read me'atsvotai, "rather than my pains," which gives a smoother sense. The first line, "my soul chooses strangling," may also hint at the choking breath of Job's illness. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew "my bones."

a: for my days are a puff of air
p: Hevel, 'breath, vapor', is the word Ecclesiastes uses for 'vanity'.
b: Hevel is a puff of breath, a vapor that vanishes. It is the key word of Ecclesiastes, traditionally "vanity" (Ecclesiastes 1:2), and the psalms use it for human life (Psalm 39:5; 144:4). Job's point is not that life is meaningless, but that it is short and slight: why should God trouble himself to hound a breath? "I give up" (ma'asti) has no object in Hebrew; he rejects or despises it, his life. The KJV's "I loathe it" catches the feeling.

a: What is a mortal, that you treat him as so great
p: Psalm 8 marvels that God cares for humans. Job complains that God will not leave him alone.
b: Psalm 8:4 asks in wonder: "What is a human being, that you remember him, a son of man, that you pay attention to him?" (author's rendering). Job takes up the same question and the same verb paqad, "attend to, visit" (7:18), but turns praise into protest: God's attention is not care but surveillance and testing. He also echoes the LORD's own words to the Accuser, "Have you set your mind on my servant Job?" (1:8): God has indeed set his mind on Job. Psalm 144:3 has a similar question. Hebrews 2:6–8 applies Psalm 8 to Jesus. Many scholars think Job 7:17–18 is a deliberate parody of the psalm.

a: let me be for the time it takes to swallow my spit
p: An idiom still used in Arabic: 'let me swallow my spit' means 'give me a moment'.
b: To "swallow one's spit" means a very short time, a breath's pause. The same expression is still used in Arabic for "wait a moment." Job does not ask God to go away forever; he asks for a moment's rest. Compare 10:20 and 14:6, where he pleads again for God to look away from him.

a: Suppose I sinned
p: The Hebrew has no 'if'. Most read it as a supposition, not a confession.
b: The Hebrew is one word, chatati, "I have sinned." The KJV reads it as a confession. Most modern translators, and the Old Greek ("if I have sinned"), take it as a supposition: even if I have sinned, what harm does it do to you? That fits Job's whole stance in these chapters, where he insists he has done nothing to deserve his suffering (6:10, 24, 30). Job does not deny being a sinner in the ordinary human sense (13:26); he denies that any sin of his can explain this.

a: you watcher of human beings
p: Notser means one who guards. It can be a loving keeper or a guard who never lets you go.
b: Notser ha'adam is "the watcher of humankind." The verb natsar usually describes God's protecting care (Psalm 12:7; Proverbs 2:8; Job 10:12 uses the synonym shamar), and the KJV renders "O thou preserver of men." In Job's mouth it is bitter: God watches him like a jailer, with his eyes always on him (7:8, 19). The same watchfulness that should be care has become a torment, as with the "fence" of 1:10 and 3:23.

a: You will search hard for me, and I will not be there
t: The last line of the speech
p: God will look for Job and not find him: a threat, a taunt, or a hint that God will miss him?
b: Job's first reply ends with a picture of God searching for him early and eagerly (shichartani, from shachar, "dawn"), and finding him gone. Readers hear it in different ways. Some hear a threat, or a taunt: if God wants to forgive, he had better hurry. Others hear a strange tenderness: Job believes that God will want him, even miss him, when he is gone. The speech that began by asking God to look away (7:19) ends by assuming that God will come looking. Job also asks for forgiveness (7:21), something only a person who still trusts God can ask. The Hebrew "and I will not be" repeats 7:8.
